card.hook: Picture a sandstone-coloured museum with Frankfurt's glass towers standing right behind it, all lined up along a leafy riverside walk. That's the Städel, and the walk is the best seat in the house.
card.stand_here: Stand on Schaumainkai, the tree-lined south bank promenade of the Main, in front of the museum row. The museum lies to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. Face the Städel so its neighbours sit in a row with the skyline rising behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the museum with the skyline behind it. Go to 0.5x if you want the whole museum row, and 2x to pick out the facade. If the building's lines start leaning in, step back and use 1x or 2x instead of 0.5x.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the museum row along the lower third, so the skyline gets the space above.
card.best_time: Aim for late afternoon, when the light is said to warm up the museum row.
card.selfie_here: Head onto the Holbeinsteg footbridge and face back toward the city so the Städel is behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it so more of the scene fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Holbeinsteg footbridge and ask a passer-by to take the photo with the Städel and its lawn in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The promenade is a street, so watch for passing cyclists and walkers while you line up your shot. Inside the museum, selfie sticks and flash aren't allowed.
card.challenge: Take three frames with different amounts of sky and skyline, then pick your favourite later over a coffee.
card.good_to_know: The Städel is one of Frankfurt's oldest museums. It was founded in 1817 after a bequest from the banker and art patron Johann Friedrich Städel. The Neo-Renaissance main building dates from 1878, was badly damaged in the Second World War and was rebuilt in 1966, and a modern underground wing opened in 2012.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Schaumainkai, the tree-lined south bank promenade of the Main, in front of the museum row. The museum lies to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. Face the Städel so its neighbours sit in a row with the skyline rising behind.

card.hook: From the street, Main Tower looks like two buildings glued together: a plain 1970s-style box next to a round tower of blue glass with a mast on top. Straight edges, curves and reflections all fit in one frame, which makes it an easy tower to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand on the streets around Main Tower in Frankfurt's Innenstadt. The phone icon marks the centre of the tower's footprint, so you'll be looking up at it from the pavement. Face the tower and step back along the street until the top fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole height in from close range. Use 1x from further back for a more natural look. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the blue glass and the spot where the two parts meet.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines and hold the phone upright, because tilting it back makes the sides lean inwards.
card.best_time: Clear daylight shows off the blue glass best. Around sunset or dusk, while the sky still has colour and the building is lit, switch on night mode and hold very still.
card.selfie_here: Try the middle of the Eiserner Steg (Iron Bridge) over the Main. A guide says the whole skyline rises up from the bridge's midpoint, mirrored in the river. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the skyline is over your shoulder. The tower can sit in the frame, but check your screen to see if it made it in.
card.ask_someone: In Taunusanlage, stand at ground level in the park and ask a passer-by to step back and aim up, so the skyscrapers around you (Main Tower among them) rise behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It can be quite windy on the Main Tower observation deck, so a nice day is the best day to go up. The viewing platforms may need a ticket or timed entry, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get one frame with both the plain box and the round blue tower in it, with the edges standing up straight against your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Main Tower is the only skyscraper in Frankfurt with a public viewing platform. It's 200 m tall, or 240 m with the antenna spire. It was built between 1996 and 1999 and is named after the nearby River Main. The foyer also has a video installation by Bill Viola and a wall mosaic by Stephan Huber.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the streets around Main Tower in Frankfurt's Innenstadt. The phone icon marks the centre of the tower's footprint, so you'll be looking up at it from the pavement. Face the tower and step back along the street until the top fits.

card.hook: Picture a 95-metre Gothic tower poking up behind a row of storybook timber houses, with a town hall squeezed in at the edge. That's the Römerberg view, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Römerberg square in Frankfurt's Old Town and face east across the square toward the cathedral tower. The half-timbered houses go in the foreground, and the Römer town hall closes in one side of the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the houses and tower sit together in one shot. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the spire. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of the square in the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Turn your phone upright, switch on the gridlines, and put the tower on a vertical line so the timber houses lead the eye up to the spire.
card.best_time: Morning is a good bet, when the light falls on the house fronts. Blue hour, when the spire is lit, is also lovely. Light changes, so check conditions on the day.
card.selfie_here: Head to Domplatz, the square in front of the cathedral's main entrance, and stand with your back to the doors. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the cathedral rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out on the open Domplatz square so they can fit the whole building in, while you stand in front of it; early morning or late afternoon is suggested for clear shots.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the cathedral, photos for personal use are generally fine, but flash is discouraged and posted restrictions apply. Visits inside or up the tower may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots of the tower: one wide, one closer, and one with a timber gable framing it. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The Dom is Frankfurt's largest religious building, but despite the English name it has never been a bishop's seat. It earned the nickname Kaiserdom because Holy Roman emperors were elected here from 1356 and crowned here from 1562 to 1792. It was built in the 14th and 15th centuries, rebuilt after a fire in 1867, then rebuilt again in the 1950s after Second World War damage.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Römerberg square in Frankfurt's Old Town and face east across the square toward the cathedral tower. The half-timbered houses go in the foreground, and the Römer town hall closes in one side of the frame.

card.hook: Here's a cheeky secret: the best photo of Frankfurt's grand old opera house has a round pond in it. The Lucae fountain catches the whole Neo-Renaissance facade in its water, so you get two Alte Operas for the price of one.
card.stand_here: Stand on Opernplatz, in front of the facade, and face the building across the Lucae fountain. Keep the fountain in the lower third of your screen and let the facade fill the rest.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and the fountain in one go. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the frieze and the upper part of the building.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then drag the brightness down a touch so the lit stonework doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go in the evening, when the square's lamps light up the facade and the fountain. Late afternoon light is also a good bet, and night mode is there if it gets dark.
card.selfie_here: Head to the granite bowl of the Lucae fountain on Opernplatz and face away from the building. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the Alte Oper facade rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the square across from the building's front while you pose by the Lucae fountain, so the facade and the fountain both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The fountain is switched off in winter, so you won't get the water reflection then. Opernplatz is open at all hours, but the inside of the Alte Oper is restricted during performances, so check the official site if you want to go in.
card.challenge: Find the words "Dem Wahren, Schönen, Guten" on the frieze and get them in a photo with the fountain below.
card.good_to_know: The architect Richard Lucae designed the Alte Oper, and it opened on 20 October 1880. Bombing in 1944 left it badly damaged, though many of the outer walls and facades survived. It was rebuilt as a concert hall and reopened on 28 August 1981, and today the Großer Saal seats 2,500 people.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Opernplatz, in front of the facade, and face the building across the Lucae fountain. Keep the fountain in the lower third of your screen and let the facade fill the rest.

card.hook: Frankfurt Hauptbahnhof isn't a quiet monument, it's a working station, and commuters hurry past while you line up your shot. It's the second busiest station in Germany, so a bit of human traffic in your photo is part of the fun.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, near Am Hauptbahnhof, about 190 m north-east of the subject. Face south-west and the station's wide front will be right ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole width of the building in. Then step in to 1x for a calmer, more natural view, and 2x for the central section and its details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the middle of the building up with the centre line and keep your phone upright so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft daylight on a clear morning or late afternoon usually gives the building front its best colour. Early on a weekend morning is usually quieter, and after dusk you can try night mode on the lit building.
card.selfie_here: Walk over to the Bahnhofsvorplatz, the square in front of the station's main facade, and turn your back on the Neo-Renaissance front. Use the front camera, switch to the wider 0.5x setting if your phone has one, and let the station rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Kaiserstraße, across from the station facade, so the whole front and the Atlas sculpture on the roof fit in the frame, while you pose on the forecourt.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay out of walkways and entrances while you shoot, as it's busy. A photo guide calls Elbestraße, near the station, one of the area's problematic streets, so stick to the forecourt. Check the official site before you go for any photography rules inside the station.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the building's vertical lines are perfectly straight and one commuter is caught mid-stride in the foreground.
card.good_to_know: The station opened on 18 August 1888 after five years of construction, and the grand entrance building was designed by Hermann Eggert. For a time it was the largest station in Europe, until Leipzig overtook it in 1915. Behind the entrance, the steel platform halls have a barrel vault about 28 metres high, and two Neoclassical outer halls were added in 1924.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon on the map, near Am Hauptbahnhof, about 190 m north-east of the subject. Face south-west and the station's wide front will be right ahead of you.

card.hook: The Eiserner Steg deck is often crowded, with people stopping for love-lock selfies every few steps. So grab your first photo from the old-town square instead, where the green-grey ironwork sits in front of the skyline.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Römerberg, at the north end where the bridge starts from the old town side. Face south, and the bridge's northern approach should be ahead of you, with the half-timbered houses beside it and the skyline behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the bridge approach, the old houses and the skyline in one frame. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more of the square. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the ironwork or the bank towers.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the bridge approach on a lower line, and keep the skyline above the horizon line.
card.best_time: Early morning on weekdays is quieter, according to one local guide. Dusk is lovely from the Sachsenhausen bank, with the bridge in front of the bank towers.
card.selfie_here: Cross to the Sachsäuser Mainufer on the Sachsenhausen bank, a few metres from the bridge. Guides say the bridge looks best from this side. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the bridge over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the Sachsenhausen riverbank a few metres from the bridge, ask a passer-by to frame the whole bridge with you standing in front.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is for pedestrians only. Check the official site for closures or photo restrictions before you go.
card.challenge: Get the half-timbered houses, the bridge and the skyline all in one shot, then walk onto the bridge and find a love lock to photograph up close.
card.good_to_know: The first iron bridge here opened in 1868. The one you see now is a cantilever bridge from 1911/1912, about 170 metres long, built from riveted steel trusses on two piers. It was blown up near the end of World War II, rebuilt in 1946 and fully renovated in 1993.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Römerberg, at the north end where the bridge starts from the old town side. Face south, and the bridge's northern approach should be ahead of you, with the half-timbered houses beside it and the skyline behind.

card.hook: Here's a fun twist: that charming front you're about to photograph is a rebuild. The original was destroyed in an Allied night raid in March 1944, and today's facade is a close copy.
card.stand_here: Stand on the opposite pavement of Großer Hirschgraben, right across from the Goethe House at number 23-25, and face the house. The phone icon on the map marks the spot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the street. If parked cars or a narrow pavement stop you stepping back, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front in.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the house with them, so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early evening, when the city lights start to come on. Use night mode and hold your phone steady against your body or a wall.
card.selfie_here: Try the courtyard garden at the back of the house, with the building's facade behind you. Use the front camera, and zoom 0.5x if you want more of the house over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the opposite pavement of Großer Hirschgraben while you stand in front of the house, so they can frame the whole building from the front.
card.rules_and_safety: The street is public, but the house is a museum. Check the official site before you go for entry and for any rules on photography inside.
card.challenge: Take three frames with different amounts of street in them, then pick the one where the neighbouring old-town buildings look best next to the house.
card.good_to_know: Goethe was born here on 28 August 1749 and grew up in the house. He also wrote Götz von Berlichingen and The Sorrows of Young Werther here. Rebuilding started in 1947, and it's now a museum with period furniture and paintings. Next door is the Deutsches Romantik-Museum, which opened in 2021.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the opposite pavement of Großer Hirschgraben, right across from the Goethe House at number 23-25, and face the house. The phone icon on the map marks the spot.

card.hook: Three stepped gables, four emperors and a clock, all squeezed onto one building: the Römer gives you plenty to point your phone at. Even the covered bridge round the side has a nickname, the 'Bridge of Sighs', because locals paid their taxes there.
card.stand_here: Stand near Markt, about 160 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Everything looks small from here, and the famous three-peaked front faces the Römerberg plaza, so walk round there for that classic view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole group of gables. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the clock, the emperors and the balcony, and hold the phone with both hands when you zoom in. Use zoom 0.5x only if you get close and want all the gables in one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the façade keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go early in the day for fewer people in your frame. Check where the sun falls on the front: bright, even light on the façade looks best, while harsh shade splits the gables.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Römerberg square and stand beside the Fountain of Justice in the middle, with the Römer façade behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x so the gables fit over your shoulder, and check the framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the Römerberg square, facing the Römer's stepped gables, while you pose by the fountain so the whole front fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The Römer is a working city hall, so check the official site before you go if you want to see inside, such as the Kaisersaal. Events and stalls can block the square, and the Römerberg Christmas market opens 23 November 2026.
card.challenge: Find the clock on the middle house, then count the four emperors above it. Bonus points for a shot that squeezes in the covered bridge too.
card.good_to_know: The city council bought the Römer from the Römer merchant family in 1405, so it has been the Rathaus for over 600 years. It is really nine houses around six courtyards. Most of it was badly damaged in March 1944 and re-opened in 1955, and the neogothic look of the façade goes back to around 1900.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Markt, about 160 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Everything looks small from here, and the famous three-peaked front faces the Römerberg plaza, so walk round there for that classic view.

card.hook: Picture a little baroque guard house, a church tower beside it and glass skyscrapers peering over its shoulder. The Hauptwache looks like it's being photobombed by the 21st century, and that's why it works so well.
card.stand_here: Start a short walk north-east of the guard house on the square An der Hauptwache, then turn and face south-west. You'll fit the guard house, the Katharinenkirche and the skyline into one picture.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x to show the whole square. Try zoom 2x to pull the church and towers in closer behind the guard house. Save zoom 0.5x for street level, when you're up close.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the church tower, so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the old stone and glass, and the square is often calmer outside the middle of the day. If you want the terrace view, pick a time when the department store is open.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the Galeria Kaufhof roof terrace (Aussichtsterrasse) on the square, if it's open. One guide says to take the escalators to the 7th floor or the lift to the 6th. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, with the Hauptwache and skyline behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of Café Hauptwache (An der Hauptwache 15) and ask a passer-by to shoot you from a few steps back across the square, with the guard house behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is public space, but the Galeria Kaufhof terrace depends on the store, so check the official site for opening times. Give people walking past a little space, especially when it's busy.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the guard house sits in the bottom third and all the glass towers loom above it, then see if you can catch a tram or a crowd crossing in front.
card.good_to_know: The Hauptwache was built in 1730 for the city's militia, and it also held a prison. It has been a café since 1904. In 1967 it was dismantled for the U-Bahn tunnel, then rebuilt over the new underground station. Most buildings around it are newer because of wartime damage, so the old guard house really stands out.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start a short walk north-east of the guard house on the square An der Hauptwache, then turn and face south-west. You'll fit the guard house, the Katharinenkirche and the skyline into one picture.

selfie_spots.why: From this terrace the Hauptwache and the skyline share one frame, so it is the strongest backdrop option on the square.

card.hook: You'll spot the Commerzbank Tower long before you arrive, so you can just walk towards the tall thing. The tricky part is fitting all of it in your phone once you're there.
card.stand_here: Stand in Kaiserplatz, the square by the tower's main entrance. The tower rises to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot away, so face north-west and look up. Check on the spot that the view matches before you settle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full height in from up close. Switch to 1x for the entrance and the lines of the lower floors. If your phone has zoom 2x to 5x, use it to pick out details higher up the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky stays blue and the glass keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Daytime gives you a clear view of the facade. At dusk and after dark the tower is lit in yellow, which makes a strong picture. Switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Eiserner Steg bridge over the River Main, where the tower is in view across the river and the old ironwork adds a vintage look. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the tower sits over your shoulder, and check the angle on the day.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Willy-Brandt-Platz facing the tower while you stand between them and the tower, which is in view across the square.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower is a working bank headquarters, so check the official site before you go if you hope to go inside.
card.challenge: Take one portrait-orientation shot with the edge of the tower lined up on a gridline, then see if your friends can guess how many storeys it has.
card.good_to_know: The tower is 259 m to the roof, or 300.1 m with its antenna spire, which makes it the tallest building in Germany. Foster & Partners designed it, and it took three years to build from 1994. It has 56 storeys and sky gardens at nine levels, and it was built in steel so those gardens could stay free of supporting columns.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Kaiserplatz, the square by the tower's main entrance. The tower rises to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot away, so face north-west and look up. Check on the spot that the view matches before you settle.

selfie_spots.why: A Frankfurt photo guide picks this bridge for an excellent view of the Commerzbank Tower against the financial district, and its ironwork adds vintage character.

card.hook: Pigeons, gables and a fountain all want to be in your photo at once, and on Römerberg they mostly get their way. Take your time, and let a few strangers wander into the frame.
card.stand_here: Near Samstagsberg, stand about 30 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-west with the fountain in front of you and the old-town buildings behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole square and the façades around it, then try 1x for a more natural view. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for gables and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain on a third line rather than dead centre, and keep the phone level so the building lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be calmer, with fewer people in the square. Later the light on the façades changes, so take a few shots. Expect crowds during the Christmas Market.
card.selfie_here: Head for the Fountain of Justice (Gerechtigkeitsbrunnen) in the middle of Römerberg. Use the front camera at 0.5x and try to get the Römer's stepped-gable façade over your shoulder, then check on the spot that it really lines up.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the square, looking straight at the Römer's stepped-gable façade, so the whole front fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed on the square, but respect private property and any rules inside individual buildings. The fountain may be covered or under restoration, and parts of the square may be fenced during the Christmas Market or other events, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the fountain on a third line, then turn around and give a different building the starring role.
card.good_to_know: The Römer has housed Frankfurt's city administration since the 15th century. The square in front of it has hosted imperial coronations, trade fairs and the Christmas Market. It was also the site of a Nazi book burning in 1933, so it's a place of memory as well as a pretty backdrop.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Near Samstagsberg, stand about 30 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-west with the fountain in front of you and the old-town buildings behind it.

selfie_spots.why: Guides name the fountain as a key photo subject on the square, and the Römer's gables sit across the square from it, so the fountain area gives a selfie with the landmark behind.

card.hook: Picture a big, round, red-sandstone building sitting at the end of an open square, like a giant terracotta pot with a lot of history. That's St. Paul's Church, and it looks best from the front of the square.
card.stand_here: Stand in Paulsplatz, the open square in front of the church's main facade, and face west. The church will fill the view, with the square spread out in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole rotunda in from the square. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for close-ups of the sandstone walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the walls so the building stands up straight, and keep a strip of square at the bottom for depth.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the stone shows its red colour. The square is open, so you can step back for the full shot.
card.selfie_here: If the big FRANKFURT letters and the bembel are still on Paulsplatz, stand next to them with the red church facade behind the sign. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the letters and the church both fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the square facing the church facade, so the whole red sandstone building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The square in front is open public space. If you want to see inside, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots of the curved wall, each from a few paces further left or right, and pick the one where the curve looks best.
card.good_to_know: Work on the church began in 1789 and finished in 1833. In 1848 and 1849 it hosted the Frankfurt National Assembly, the first parliament for the whole of Germany. It was destroyed in March 1944, and it was the first building Frankfurt rebuilt after the war. Today it's used for exhibitions and events, not as a working church.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Paulsplatz, the open square in front of the church's main facade, and face west. The church will fill the view, with the square spread out in front of you.

card.hook: Most museum visits happen indoors, but this one is a whole riverbank of them, with the Frankfurt skyline across the water as a free backdrop. You can wander it and never buy a ticket, just take photos.
card.stand_here: Stand on Schaumainkai, on the stretch running downriver toward the Untermainbrücke. The museum embankment lies to the north-west, so face that way with the river in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the long embankment, the river and the skyline into one shot. Use 1x for the museum fronts, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out towers and details across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the river edge or promenade along the lower third line so it leads the eye along the embankment.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Skip Saturdays if you want it quiet, because the flea market partly closes the street to traffic.
card.selfie_here: Try the rooftop terrace of the Museum für Kommunikation on Schaumainkai, which the Museumsuferfest describes as a spot for selfies with the skyscrapers. The Eiserner Steg bridge is another popular photo spot with views of both the Museumsufer and the skyline. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt it so the skyline fits in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Schaumainkai pavement opposite the Städel Museum, while you stand to one side of its facade so the museum row along the river fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The embankment is an open public street and promenade, but individual museums are ticketed and some events close parts of it, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a spot where an old villa front and a modern museum building sit side by side, and get both in one shot.
card.good_to_know: Museumsufer isn't one building but a long stretch of the Main riverbank lined with museums on both sides, with the Städel art museum at its centre. Most of the others were added in the 1980s under the city's culture chief Hilmar Hoffmann, some in converted villas and some in new buildings. By 2022 there were 39 museums.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Schaumainkai, on the stretch running downriver toward the Untermainbrücke. The museum embankment lies to the north-west, so face that way with the river in front of you.

card.hook: Stand in the middle of the Römerberg and turn slowly: stepped gables, a cathedral tower, and a long pale sandstone building that just keeps going. That's the Schirn, and the whole scene fits in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Römerberg, the square itself, and face the Schirn's long sandstone facade. Keep the Römer's stepped gables on one side and let the cathedral tower rise behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the facade and the square. If it feels cramped, go to 0.5x, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the gables or the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the facade up with a horizontal line, then leave a bit of sky above the tower.
card.best_time: We can't promise a quiet hour here, so go when it suits you. If the square is busy, wait a moment for a gap and take your shot then.
card.selfie_here: Stand among the square pillars along the northern façade with the Schirn behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more in, and hold the phone a little high. The pillars are a popular photo spot, including for couples married at the nearby Römer registry office.
card.rules_and_safety: The Schirn's main building is being renovated, so scaffolding or banners may block the facade. If they do, try the colonnaded walkway beside the building, where the cathedral is close by, and check the official site before you go. Photo rules inside change from show to show, so ask before you shoot indoors.
card.challenge: Get the facade straight on the gridline, the gables on one side and the cathedral tower peeking over the top, then add your best 'I found it' grin.
card.good_to_know: The Schirn opened in 1986 on ground that was flattened in the Second World War and left empty for decades. 'Schirn' is an old word for an open-air market stall, and butchers' stalls stood in the lanes here until the 19th century. The main hall is about 140 metres long and five storeys high, and the glass-domed rotunda at the entrance is about 20 metres across.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Römerberg, the square itself, and face the Schirn's long sandstone facade. Keep the Römer's stepped gables on one side and let the cathedral tower rise behind.

card.hook: Picture a 600-year-old stone tower with a steep spire and four tiny corner turrets, and a glass high-rise standing right behind it like it's photobombing history. That's the Eschenheimer Turm, and the Nextower behind it is what makes the shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the plaza called Eschenheimer Tor, in front of the tower, and face it so the Nextower rises directly behind it. Traffic and street furniture love to sneak in here, so take a few steps left or right and check the edges of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the tower with the Nextower behind it. Try 0.5x if you want all 47 metres in the frame from close by, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) from further back to squeeze the two buildings closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go at a quieter time of day, such as early morning, so there are fewer people and vehicles in your picture. Check what the site looks like first, because building work nearby can spoil the view.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone level so the tower stands up straight behind your shoulder. Take a few tries, since the busy plaza changes the background every time.
card.ask_someone: Walk along Eschersheimer Landstraße and turn around: you stand in front of the tower, and your photographer stands on the street facing it, so you both fit in with the Nextower behind.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza and the outside of the tower are open public space. The inside is a restaurant and any battlement visit may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the two carved coats of arms, a silver eagle on red and a black double-headed eagle on gold, and get a zoomed photo of each.
card.good_to_know: The tower is 47 metres high, with a square base holding the gate arch and a round tower on top. Master builder Madern Gerthener finished it in 1426–1428. When the old city walls came down in the early 1800s, it was one of only three towers allowed to stay. Up top, the weather vane has holes from a famous legend about a poacher and nine pistol shots, though the vane isn't the original.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the plaza called Eschenheimer Tor, in front of the tower, and face it so the Nextower rises directly behind it. Traffic and street furniture love to sneak in here, so take a few steps left or right and check the edges of your screen.

ask_someone_spot.name: Eschersheimer Landstraße, looking back toward the tower
ask_someone_spot.detail: Walk along Eschersheimer Landstraße and turn around. From there the tower and the Nextower behind it are seen together. The visitor stands in front of the tower, and the photographer stands on the street facing it.

sources.title: Frankfurt: Die 16 schönsten Fotospots (coeser.de)

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor stands with the Eschenheimer Turm behind them, so selfie_spots is empty. The blog's recommended viewpoint is a look back from Eschersheimer Landstraße, which puts the tower in front of the camera, so it is listed as the passer-by spot instead. The blog also warns that the scene is hard to shoot cleanly because of disturbing elements in the frame. A Tripadvisor reviewer says it is hard to find a spot to photograph the full tower because it is surrounded by a busy road. Rooftop views of the tower exist at the Fleming's hotel (Occhio d'Oro restaurant, 7th floor, and the Fleming's Club area), but those are indoor or private venues rather than public spots, and the pages do not describe a selfie there. No page states rules about selfie sticks or tripods.

card.hook: Picture a tall brick Gothic tower with a few cosy half-timbered houses tucked in beside it, like a postcard that came to life. That's Old St. Nicholas Church from the Römerberg, and it's the shot everyone wants.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Römerberg, the old town square in Frankfurt's Altstadt, close to the Römer city hall. Face the church on the south side of the square, so the brick facade and tower fill the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the facade, the tower and the neighbouring half-timbered houses in one frame. Go to zoom 0.5x if you want the top of the tower and more of the square, but keep the church away from the very edge, where buildings can look stretched. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the brickwork and tower details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the building doesn't lean, and tap the brickwork to set the shot. If the sky is bright, drag the slider to make it a little darker so the facade keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is best, when the sun lights the building, according to one photography guide. The square can get busy in the daytime, so be patient and wait for a gap between people.
card.selfie_here: Try the open part of the Römerberg by the Fountain of Justice (Gerechtigkeitsbrunnen), with the church on the south side of the square behind you. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and hold your phone so the church tower peeks over your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot to make sure the church really lines up behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the square in front of the Römer town hall and shoot south, while you stand in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: The Römerberg is an open public square, but the church itself holds services and events, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead straight against a gridline, with a couple of half-timbered houses at the edge of the frame and not a stranger's head in sight. Patience wins this one!
card.good_to_know: The first chapel on this site was built in the mid-12th century, and the church you see now dates from the mid-15th. It has 51 bells, and 47 of them are used for carillons. The old town around it was heavily damaged in World War II, but this church came through with only minor damage.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Römerberg, the old town square in Frankfurt's Altstadt, close to the Römer city hall. Face the church on the south side of the square, so the brick facade and tower fill the middle of your screen.

selfie_spots.why: A travel guide names the Fountain of Justice as a photo subject near the church, and the church is the square's centerpiece, but no page says the church is directly behind a visitor at this exact spot.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot could be supported. No page names a spot where a visitor stands with the church directly behind them; the Fountain of Justice is named only as a nearby photo subject, so check the framing on site. The ask-someone spot relies on the Römer being opposite the church on the square, which two pages state, but no page gives a exact standing point. No page states rules on selfie sticks or tripods, so none are reported. A page says flash should be avoided inside the church during services, but that is a general photography rule, not a selfie-stick/tripod rule, so it is not listed. The provided coordinates (50.10995, 8.68234) sit close to the church; one photo page lists a camera position at about 50.110390, 8.682353.

card.hook: Picture a street where every house is wearing a different outfit: pastel fronts, dark beams, steep gables squeezed side by side. That's the New Old Town, and it's tiny, so you'll be hunting for details rather than a big sweeping view.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Hühnermarkt, the little square at the centre of the New Old Town. From the Römerberg, walk east into the quarter, about 60 m (roughly a minute's walk). Face the reconstructed half-timbered and pastel facades.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole square and the rows of facades into one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for carved timber and gable details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the house edges so the tall, narrow houses stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people wandering through your shot. Have a look at how the light falls on the facades while you're there.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of the Hühnermarkt with the reconstructed house fronts behind you, front camera at 0.5x so plenty of facade fits in. For a fancier backdrop, try standing in front of the Haus zur Goldenen Waage, the Renaissance house in the quarter.
card.rules_and_safety: The quarter is public streets and squares. Check the official site before you go for events or closures.
card.challenge: Find the steepest gable in the square and get it in your shot with a pastel house right beside it.
card.good_to_know: Before the Second World War bombing, Frankfurt had around 1,250 timber-framed buildings, one of the biggest collections anywhere. This quarter was rebuilt between 2012 and 2018 and opened fully on 9 May 2018. About 35 building designs were picked through architectural competitions, which is why the facades all look so different.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Hühnermarkt, the little square at the centre of the New Old Town. From the Römerberg, walk east into the quarter, about 60 m (roughly a minute's walk). Face the reconstructed half-timbered and pastel facades.

selfie_spots.why: Visit Frankfurt names the Hühnermarkt among the New Old Town's photo backdrops, and Tall Girl Big World calls it a pretty photo op in the middle of the quarter.
